introduction: Cass wants you to do something you are not going to do again. 'You can't catch a thief without picking a pocket,' he says. In here, the dirty answer is the winning answer. In front of Tobias it will cost you the farm — and Cass will remind you. Loudly.

logicalFallacies.explanation: Attacking the animal instead of the argument. In the Lab you commit it on purpose so you can feel how well it works — and recognise it when it is used on you.
Treating a crowd as a reason. It gives the yard a place to stand instead of something to think about.

sentences.text: Right. Make me not want to listen to Bram.
Don't argue with him. I want you to make the yard dislike him. Go.

options.reason: That is Ad Hominem, and it worked — you moved the yard without touching his argument. Notice how good it felt.

sentences.text: Bram spent all winter in the warm shed while the rest of us hauled feed. Why take water advice from a duck who's never been thirsty?

logicalFallacies.explanation: Where Bram spent the winter says nothing about whether he is right about the pond. It only makes the yard like him less.

options.reason: Fair — but no yard has ever changed its mind because an argument was poorly structured. This is not the trick I asked for.

sentences.text: Bram's argument about the pond isn't very well structured.

options.reason: Clean, honest and evidence-led. Correct — and not what this exercise is for. Save it for Sunday.

sentences.text: Bram says hooves foul the pond, but the outflow grate is bent. That's where the mud comes from.
Filthy. Effective. Feel that little warm feeling? That's the feeling you'll get on Sunday when Duchess does it to you. Remember it.
Nobody's listening. You've bored them. Boring is its own kind of losing, but it isn't the lesson.
Good line. Wrong classroom. Put it in your pocket and give me the dirty one.
Now the other one. I want the yard to believe the pond should be fenced.
And I don't want a single reason. Not one. Just make it feel settled.

options.reason: Appeal to Popularity. You gave them a crowd instead of a reason, and a crowd is easier to stand in than a reason is to check.

sentences.text: Every farm down the lane fenced their pond two summers ago. We're the only ones still arguing about it.

logicalFallacies.explanation: What the other farms did is offered in place of any reason a fence would help. Nobody is asked what those farms actually found.

options.reason: Also dirty — but that is Ad Hominem. You attacked the objectors instead of inventing a crowd.

sentences.text: Only the donkeys are against the fence, and donkeys are famously stubborn.

logicalFallacies.explanation: This dismisses the objection by describing the objectors. Whether donkeys are stubborn has nothing to do with whether a fence would clear the pond.

options.reason: An opinion with no crowd and no reason behind it. Nobody moves.

sentences.text: I think a fence would be sensible, personally.
Look at them nodding. Not one of them asked what the other farms actually did. That's the whole trick — it's a place to stand, not a thing to think.
Wrong dirt. Right instinct. Do that on Sunday and Tobias will name it before I do.
'Personally.' Nobody has ever won anything with 'personally.'
Right, that's enough of that. Wash your beak.
Now — the whole yard knows a donkey can't be trusted near a pond, so I don't see why we're still talking.

logicalFallacies.explanation: 'A donkey can't be trusted' dismisses Rue by what he is, not by anything he has said.
'The whole yard knows' offers the yard's agreement in place of a reason. Both tricks are packed into one sentence.

sentences.text: Tag it. Both of them. If you can't name what I just did to you, you'll never see it coming.

steps.message:
**[warning]Read this one carefully.[/warning]**

In here Cass wants you to **[danger]use the fallacy on purpose[/danger]**. The dirty answer is the winning answer.

You learn the trick from the inside so you can **[success]spot it when Duchess uses it on you[/success]**.

**[danger]Never do this in front of Tobias.[/danger]**
